Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM3124 : Biosensors and Biotransducers { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Fundamentals of Instrumentation and Transducers
Introduction to electrical quantities and units. Functional elements of instrumentation systems. Static and dynamic characteristics: Accuracy, precision, resolution, sensitivity, drift, and hysteresis. Analog and digital measurement principles: CRO, energy meters, time and frequency meters, and multimeters. Classification of transducers: Resistive strain gauges, RTD, LVDT, piezoelectric, electromagnetic, and optical transducers. Applications of transducers in biomedical science.
Module 2: Generalized Instrumentation and Measurement Techniques
General properties and design criteria for input transducers. Static characteristics: Linearity, reproducibility, input/output impedance. Dynamic characteristics: First-order and second-order systems, transfer functions, time delay, error-free instruments. Measurement of displacement, motion, and pressure: Resistive elements: Potentiometers, strain gauges, and bridge circuits. Inductive elements: Variable inductance and LVDT. Capacitive and piezoelectric elements. Types of diaphragms, bellows, and Bourdon tubes. Temperature measurement: Thermistors, thermocouples, RTDs, IC-based sensors, and radiation sensors.
Module 3: Biopotential Electrodes and Interfaces
Electrodes-electrolyte interface: Half-cell potential, polarization, and electrode impedance. Polarizable and non-polarizable electrodes. Electrode circuit models and motion artifacts. Body surface electrodes, internal electrodes (needle and wire types), and microelectrodes (metal and micropipette-based). Applications in ECG, EEG, and EMG monitoring.
Module 4: Chemical Sensors and Biosensors
Blood gas and acid-base physiology sensors: pH, pO2, pCO2 electrodes. Potentiometric and amperometric sensors. Ion-selective electrodes, ISFETs, and Clark electrodes. Fiber optic sensors: Principles and applications in temperature, chemical, and pressure sensing. Biosensor classifications: Biological and transduction phenomena. Enzyme-based and electrode-based sensors, catalytic biosensors, and immunosensors.
Module 5: Advanced Biosensor Technologies and Applications
Design and fabrication of fiber optic sensors. Integration of biosensors in clinical and industrial applications. Non-invasive biosensors for blood-gas and glucose monitoring. Applications of biosensors in the bioprocess industry and environmental analysis. Introduction to biochips and their applications in genomics and diagnostics. Case studies on advanced biosensors and emerging trends.

Course Objective

1 .

To provide a comprehensive understanding of instrumentation systems, transducers, and their static and dynamic characteristics for biomedical and industrial applications.
2 .

To explore the principles and applications of biopotential electrodes, chemical sensors, and biosensors, with a focus on their role in biomedical monitoring and diagnostics.
3 .

To develop an in-depth understanding of measurement techniques for displacement, motion, pressure, and temperature using advanced transducers.
4 .

To introduce students to advanced biosensor technologies, including non-invasive monitoring systems and biochips, for clinical, industrial, and environmental applications.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Analyze the functional elements and performance characteristics of instrumentation systems and transducers for precise measurements.
2. Demonstrate the ability to select and apply appropriate sensors and transducers for measuring physical and physiological quantities in biomedical and industrial contexts.
3. Design and implement biopotential electrode systems for monitoring ECG, EEG, and EMG signals with minimal interference and artifacts.
4. Evaluate the principles and applications of chemical sensors and biosensors in real-world biomedical, industrial, and environmental scenarios.
5. Integrate advanced biosensor technologies, such as biochips and fiber-optic sensors, into innovative solutions for diagnostics, monitoring, and process control.

Essential Reading

1 .

Richard S.C. Cobbold, Transducers for Biomedical Measurements: Principles and Applications, John Wiley & Sons

2 .

Harry N, Norton, Biomedical sensors – fundamentals and application, Harry N, Norton

Supplementary Reading

1 .

I. Sinclair, Sensors and Transducers: A Guide for Technicians, Newnes

2 .

T. R. Padmanabhan, Industrial Instrumentation: Principles and Design, Springer

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE2003 : Mechanics of Solids { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I: Concept of Stress and Strain [9 hours]
Definition of stress, Normal and Shearing stresses and corresponding strains in axially loaded members, Stress-Strain relationship and its diagram for uniaxial loading for ductile and brittle materials, Stress tensor, Generalised Hooke's Law, Poisson's ratio, relationship between elastic constants, Working stress, Factor of safety. Composite bars in tension and compression, temperature stresses in composite rods, statically indeterminate problems in axial tension and compression.
Module II: Thin Cylinders and Spherical Shells [4 hours]
Bi-axial Stresses in thin cylinders and thin spherical shells under internal pressure, wire winding of thin cylinders.
Module III: Transformation of Plane Stress and Plane Strain [6 hours]
Two dimensional state of stress, principal stresses and principal planes, Mohr's circle of stress, Two dimensional state of strain, principal strains and principal axes of strain, Mohr's circle of strain, measurement of strain by strain gauge and strain rosettes, determination of principal strains from strain measurements, calculation of principal stresses from principal strains.
Module IV: Torsion of Circular Shafts and Helical Springs [5 hours]
Torsion formula, strength of solid and hollow circular shafts, design of circular members in torsion, power transmitted, and close coiled helical springs.
Module V: Analysis of beams [9 hours]
Members subjected to flexural loads, relationships between load, shearing force and bending moment, shear force and bending moment diagrams of cantilever and simply supported beams, elastic curve. Theory of simple and non-uniform bending of initially straight beams, bending stresses in beams, shearing stresses in beams, beams of two materials, carriage springs. Slope and deflection of beams by integration method and moment area method.
Module VI: Theory of Columns [3 hours]
Euler's theory for initially straight columns with various end conditions, eccentric loading of columns, stresses in short struts with eccentric loading, Kern of rectangular and circular sections.

Course Objective

1 .

To understand the fundamental concepts of stress and strain and their relationship, working stress, Factor of safety, temperature stresses, Bi-axial Stresses in thin cylinders and thin spherical shells under internal pressure, wire winding, Transformation of Plane Stress and Plane Strain
2 .

Analysis and design of shafts and close coiled helical springs subject to torsional load.
3 .

Analysis of beams subjected to flexural loads, relationships between load, shearing force and bending moment, shear force and bending moment diagrams of cantilever and simply supported beams, elastic curve. Theory of simple and non-uniform bending of initially straight beams, bending stresses in beams, shearing stresses in beams, beams of two materials. Slope and deflection of beams by integration method and moment area method.
4 .

Understand the concept of buckling, Stability of short and long columns.

Course Outcome

1 .

After the completion of this course, students will be able to:
CO1: Have an idea on the performance of deformable solids of various materials under the action of different kind of loads, Understand the fundamental concepts of stress and strain and the relationship between them through the strain-stress equations, temperature stresses.
CO2: Know the stresses in thin cylinders and thin spherical shells under internal pressure, strengthen thin cylinders and spheres by wire winding, perform transformation of Plane Stress and Plane Strain.
CO3: Analyse and design shafts subject to torsional load and close coiled helical springs subject to axial loads.
CO4: Analyse beams subject to flexure loads.
CO5: Understand the concept of buckling, Stability of short and long columns.

2 .

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CS3006 : Distributed Systems { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Introduction to Distributed systems: Review of Networks, Operating Systems, Concurrent Programming, and Characteristics & Properties of Distributes Systems – Taxonomy - Design goals – Transparency Issues
Distributed Computing Paradigms: Basic Message Passing Model – The Client Server, Message Passing, RPC basics, RPC implementation, RPC communication and issues, Remote Procedure Call Model – RPC in conventional languages and in Java - The Distributed Objects – The Collaborative Application
Inter process communication mechanisms: Communication in Distributed Systems, Socket Programming -Client Server examples, I/O Multiplexing, Inetd Super Server – Secure Sockets – The SSL & the Java Secure Socket Extension
Process models in distributed systems: Processes, Threads - Code Migration Software Agents – CSP Distributed Processes - Naming with Mobile Entities - Unreferenced Objects
Synchronization: Clock Synchronization – Logical clocks – Election Algorithms – Distributed Mutual Exclusion
Consistency and Replication: Motivation, Object Replication, Consistency Models, Distribution Protocols , Consistency Protocols
Fault Tolerance: Failure Models – Process Resilience – Reliable Client Server and Group Communications – Distributed Commit Protocols – Check-pointing and Recovery - Distributed Databases - Distributed Transactions
Distributed File System: File system, DFS- definition, Characteristics, Goals, SUN NFS-NFS Architecture, NFS Implementation, Protocols, The CODA file system-Design Overview, An Example, Design Rational, Implementation, The GOOGLE file system-Definition, Architectures, GFS Architecture

Course Objective

1 .

To learn the principles, architectures, algorithms and programming models used in distributed systems.
2 .

To examine state-of-the-art distributed systems, such as Google File System.
3 .

To design and implement sample distributed systems
4 .

Students will gain an understanding of the principles and techniques behind the design of distributed systems, such as locking, concurrency, scheduling, and communication across networks. Second, students will gain practical experience in designing, implementing, and debugging real distributed systems.

demonstrate knowledge of the basic elements and concepts related to distributed system technologies
demonstrate knowledge of the core architectural aspects of distributed systems

Syllabus

Basics of weather models Different spatial and temporal scales in NWP, Basic structure of numerical models and their applications, Governing equations, Map projections, Vertical coordinate system Global models, Regional models, Mesoscale models, Hydrostatic & non-hydrostatic assumption. Subject {L-T-P / C} : MA4103 : Complex Analysis - II { 3-1-0 / 4}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1(10 hours) Complex Functions, Spherical representations of extended complex plane, Analytic functions, Cauchy Riemann equations, Harmonic functions, Branches of multiple-valued functions, Branch point and Branch cut.
Module 2(10 hours) Complex Integral, Cauchy Goursat theorem, Cauchy's integral formula, Simply connected domain, Independence of paths.
Module 3 (10 hours ) Power Series, Taylor series, Laurent series, zeros and singularities, Residue calculus, Cauchy residue theorem, Evaluation of definite integrals, Argument principle, Rouches theorem.
Module 4 (10 hours) Conformal mappings, Geometry of Mobius transformations, Open mapping theorem, Maximum modulus theorem, Schwarz’s lemma, Partial fractions and factorization, Entire Functions, Picard Theorem.

Course Objective

1 .

To provide an overview of what is complex analysis and why it is important to study. To motivate how one can use the theory of complex analysis for evaluating many real analysis problems comfortably.
2 .

To introduce analytic functions, complex integral, entire functions, conformal mappings, singularities, mapping theorems and their applications.
3 .

To provide the fundamental concepts of complex analysis and
point out the differences between real and complex in each context.
4 .

To motivate for higher studies in advance complex analysis.

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1: Students will learn complex differentiation, multivalued functions, analytic and harmonic functions.
CO2: Students will learn to compute complex integration and evaluate the definite integral.
CO3:They will learn the singularities and zeros of complex functions and will be able to evaluate their residues.
CO4: Students will learn the conformal maps and Mobius transformations.
CO5: Students will have the knowledge and skills to solve problems independently. They will have the ability to use techniques from complex analysis and apply them to diverse fields like PDEs, Real Analysis, Fourier Transforms, and Analytic Number Theory.

J. B. Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable, Springer , 1978

2 .

T. W. Gamelin, Complex Analysis, Springer , 2000

Supplementary Reading

J.E. Marsden and M.J. Hoffman, Basic Complex Analysis, W H Freeman & Co , 1998
